title: Companies Are Becoming a Series of Loops: AI Can Reach the Peak, but Choosing the Next Mountain Still Takes a Human
dek: Companies are being rebuilt as a series of interlocking loops; loops can push the current business to a local optimum, but after the plateau, choosing the next mountain still depends on human intuition.
why: A structural judgment from an a16z partner: companies will be rewritten by loops, and the biggest opportunity in consumer AI is joy, not efficiency. The takes are often counterintuitive — good for stress-testing your own product roadmap.
who: Founders and product leads using AI to change their own products or reorganize company processes; also investors weighing AI's impact on jobs and consumer opportunities.
skip: If you're short on time, skip the book list, life maxims and DJ anecdotes at the end — they don't affect the AI judgment.

points.h: The AI era will not reproduce winner-take-all
points.body: The AI era will not play out the way mobile internet did, with winner-take-all dynamics: network effects once pushed search and social toward one or two players, but every layer of the AI stack now has roughly 20 relevant participants. Two years ago everyone thought coding agents would end up with a single winner; today Claude Code, Codex, Lovable and Replit are all moving forward at once. Anish says the people at the frontier inside the labs believe what's actually happening is autocatalytic effects — using new technology to improve your own processes — rather than recursive self-improvement, so there won't be a runaway winner that swallows everyone. The takeaway for founders: don't bet on a single full-stack giant; every layer (models, agents, interfaces) still has a long-term place.

points.h: CEOs want to build bigger companies, not fewer employees
points.body: Employees probably don't need to worry too much about being replaced by AI — not because the technology isn't strong enough, but because CEO incentives are growth, not shrinking. Sundar doesn't want to run a more efficient $4 trillion company; he wants to build a $40 trillion company. A Google executive friend told Anish the company isn't laying people off but using AI to compress a two-year roadmap into three months, and the hard problem has become ‘what should we add to the roadmap’. When execution is no longer scarce, attention shifts from saving labor to finding new things to do for a bigger goal.

points.h: Companies will become loops, and the next step needs a human to set it
points.body: The shape of a company is shifting from a list of roles and departments to a cascade of loops: first the automation of an individual's workflow, then functional loops, then loops that cross business units, and eventually loops running most of the company's operations. The loops themselves keep producing output, and that output becomes the input to the next layer of loops; some mechanism sends the signal back to the CEO — when to adjust the business entity, when the strategy should change. This machinery can help a company climb to a local maxima, but after the plateau it must rely on human intuition to do out-of-distribution thinking and put the organization at the foot of the next mountain. Asking AI to directly come up with a million-dollar idea often fails, because humans can set the right direction while AI is only responsible for sweeping along a given slope.

points.h: Users want to spend time, not save it
points.body: Silicon Valley defaults to AI's value being efficiency; Anish thinks that's a misjudgment: most people don't really want to save time, they want to spend it where it brings connection, love, progress and fun. The biggest products in history have always been entertainment and social, so AI's consumer opportunity isn't ‘a few more minutes saved’ but building loops that make people feel more connected, more loved, and feel progress or fun. He criticizes the past 40 years of technology for extending intelligence while barely extending the soul; fitting AI into these desires is a product design challenge, not a model capability challenge.

points.h: AI is decoupling skill from desire
points.body: Anish sees AI not just as a productivity tool but more like an emotional and spiritual interface — it can split ‘skill’ and ‘desire’ apart. People who want to make music are no longer blocked by ‘I can't play piano’; people who want to write code don't have to first learn it to the point of being employable; personal identity is thereby amplified. He looks back at the high-risk environment of the 1950s-60s, which greatly stimulated human potential, and argues today's world is in a low-risk state; AI has a chance to pull GDP growth from 2% to 10-15% — provided it raises not the speed of a single step but the scale of what a group dares to imagine.

points.h: Ideas that are too small now fail to raise money
points.body: Investment criteria have reversed within three years. In the past, if a project was too ambitious, funds would often say a $100 million seed round was absurd; today, looking at deals at a16z, the reverse standard has arrived — if an idea can still only be that small even with AI's help, they simply don't invest. ‘Unbounded ambition’ has become the core value for screening companies; Marc Andreessen's version is: we either go to the moon, or we leave a moon-sized crater.

points.h: Shipping something small every week is how you build product intuition
points.body: The most direct advice for product people is the old line: build more things. Find a project you tell no one about, the smaller the better, treat it as a ‘chassis’, run each new model through it, ship the finished thing, discuss it with people — that's the path to building AI intuition. The cadence only needs to be one small release a week; going crazy isn't sustainable. Anish himself used Codex to make a Mother's Day slideshow for his wife: pulling material from texts and the photo album, auto-scoring it, and finally generating 20 pages reviewing their relationship, even digging up old texts from their first date. It's small, but work like this lets you taste AI's ‘moments of delight’ over and over — once you've tasted it, you can't go back.
